extracted.intended_audience: Students of painting (Royal Academy students); practicing painters and art students
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for producing the 'great' (grand) style of painting — especially history painting — covering invention, composition, colour, drapery, expression, and how lesser genres relate to the grand style. Advice is directed at students learning to prioritise general ideas over minute particularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of art proportional to mental labour/pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The value and rank of every art is in proportion to the mental labour employed in it, or the mental pleasure produced by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes 'liberal art' from 'mechanical trade' — works addressed to nobler faculties or producing higher mental pleasure are of higher rank. Evaluate artworks by the depth of intellectual engagement and the mental effect on the spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer general ideas over particularities (ideal beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect form is produced by leaving out particularities, and retaining only general ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to represent the general idea of things rather than minute, local, or temporary details. Reducing particulars gives the 'grand style' its permanence and universal appeal. Anti-pattern: over-attending to specificity that breaks the unity of the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject — general interest / heroic nature
rubrics_metrics.description: No subject can be proper that is not generally interesting; it ought to be some eminent instance of heroic action or heroic suffering, or otherwise of universal concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects widely known and emotionally available to the public (e.g., Greco-Roman history, Scripture). Avoid narrow, local, or trivial incidents when aspiring to history painting or the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject unembarrassed by distracting particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that the subject selected should be kept unembarrassed with whatever may any way serve to divide the attention of the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding dress, furniture, and scene, contrive them so they strike the spectator no more than they did in the initial mental picture. Use minute details sparingly and only when they serve truth or grandeur; otherwise sacrifice them to the greater whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination — subordinate parts must not compete with the principal
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate actions, groups, and masses of light should not come into any degree of competition with the principal; they should form part of the whole and be necessary to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure subsidiary figures/lights support, rather than distract from, the central idea. Evaluate whether each subordinate element is essential — 'show that they must be there' — and whether they remain subordinate in impact and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of means — avoid ostentation of technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter is to make no ostentation of the means by which the effect is produced; the spectator is only to feel the result in his bosom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great artists conceal the labour and artifice of composition, drapery, and lighting so these do not occur to memory unprompted. Anti-pattern: works where mechanism is boastfully displayed — 'boastful art and open affectation'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm and determined outline; correctness of general form
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm and determined outline is one of the characteristics of the great style in painting; he who possesses knowledge of the exact form will express that knowledge with correctness and precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain clear, decisive drawing of general forms even while omitting trivial specifics. Precision of essential form is a mark of mastery; do not confuse omission of particulars with looseness of draftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression should reflect general situation and social rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Those expressions alone should be given to the figures which their respective situations generally produce; each person should also have that expression which men of his rank generally exhibit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give figures expressions that are universal for the passion and appropriate to their social or heroic status. Avoid idiosyncratic or accidental expressions that are not general or dignified (example: Bernini's biting under-lip mistaken for universality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetical licence to ennoble historical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter sometimes ought to deviate from vulgar and strict historical truth in pursuing the grandeur of his design; this is an allowed poetical licence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For history painting, adjust physical traits or incidental facts when necessary to convey dignity and the moral or heroic character (e.g., not depicting Alexander's low stature). This is not falsification but a legitimate means to the ‘poetical’ representation of the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouring: simplicity, breadth, and overall quietness
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a general air of grandeur at first view, all trifling or artful play of little lights or attention to a variety of tints is to be avoided; a quietness and simplicity must reign over the whole work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broad, simple colour harmonies to create an immediate, majestic effect. Avoid excessive small highlights or busy tint variety that distracts from the primary impression. Evaluate by first-glance impact and uniform breadth of colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two valid colour strategies for grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandeur of effect is produced by two different ways: (1) by reducing the colours to little more than chiaroscuro (Bolognian practice), or (2) by making the colours very distinct and forcible (Roman/Florentine). The presiding principle of both is simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both restrained chiaroscuro and vivid, distinct colours can achieve grandeur so long as overall simplicity, unity, and purpose are preserved. Do not confuse variety of method with lack of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery treated as drapery, not as specific fabric detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In the great style the clothing is neither woollen, linen, nor silk: it is drapery; it is nothing more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose folds and clothing to present graceful, continuous forms that serve the figure and overall composition, rather than to catalogue materials. Aim for flowing outline and 'natural negligence' so drapery conceals artifice and reveals the figure to advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of drapery requires nicest judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of disposing the foldings of the drapery makes a very considerable part of the painter's study; it requires the nicest judgment to make folds communicate easily and gracefully while showing the figure to its utmost advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drapery as a compositional device requiring taste and judgment, not mere mechanical replication of cloth behavior. Antipattern: drapery painted merely 'natural' as a mechanical operation without grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing incompatible styles (grand vs ornamental)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles by which [the grand] style and the ornamental (Venetian) style are attained are so contrary that they seem incompatible; the union is more imperfect than either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve stylistic uniformity: choose to pursue either the grave, majestic 'grand style' or the elegant, ornamental style and avoid attempted blends that dilute both. Composite styles risk affectation or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach portraits differently from history painting
rubrics_metrics.description: A portrait painter retains individual likeness; a painter of history shows the man by showing his actions. A portrait attempts a particular man, a history painter aims at man in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting portraits, prioritize recognizable likeness and the sitter's character; when painting history/political/religious scenes prioritize universal, idealized representation to convey the action and moral meaning. Beware letting portrait habits make historical heads look like mere portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of figures — prefer one complete whole to many small parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime impresses the mind at once with one great idea; many little things will not make a great one. Annibale Caracci thought twelve figures sufficient for any story; excessive numbers often only 'fill space'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose so the work reads as a single powerful idea rather than an accumulation of minor incidents. Excessive figures risk creating 'figures to be let' — detached or peripheral figures that weaken unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid local/national particularity in history painting
rubrics_metrics.description: History pieces become improper when they are portraits of the painter's own people, exhibiting minute national particularities that do not give a general view of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or neutralize narrowly local costumes, gestures, or lighting that make a history painting feel parochial. History painting should aim at universality; local colour is fine for lower genres but contaminates grand history pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape as composed ideal rather than slavish copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking nature as he found it seldom produced beauty; landscapes can be compositions of various draughts from beautiful scenes rather than faithful portraits of one spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For noble landscape, recombine and idealize elements from multiple studies to achieve a general beauty and repose. Avoid slavish representation of accidental peculiarities that break the composed tranquillity of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate technical excellence for lesser subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: For humbler walks (portraits, domestic scenes, landscapes, animals, still life), qualities like colouring, handling (lightness of pencil), and skilful management of light and shadow are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that lesser genres demand their own highest attainments (e.g., still life and flower painting need brilliancy and delicate handling). Do not disparage these skills, but place them in the appropriate rank and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and constancy of presiding principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one presiding principle which regulates every art: works built upon general nature live forever, while those depending on particular customs, partial views, or fashion are coeval with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works by whether they are founded on general nature (timeless) or on transient particulars. Prioritise generality and universality as the principle that gives stability and lasting value to art.
